title: 12V USB charging station
summary: Power several phones, radios and lights from a 12V battery using salvaged car USB chargers or buck-converter boards, fused at the battery. Car chargers already handle the phone handshake, so they are the easy choice.

materials.item: Car USB chargers (cigarette-lighter plugs) or buck-converter boards (LM2596 type)
12V sockets to plug car chargers into, or USB sockets for bare boards
Fuse and holder, 5–10A, within 30 cm of battery +
Wire 16–14 AWG (1.5–2.5 mm²), red and black
Board or box to mount everything on
Small panel voltmeter to watch the battery

steps.text: Test each car charger: plug it into a 12V source and measure 5.0–5.25V between the outer pins of the USB socket (pin 1 positive, pin 4 negative). Scrap any that read wrong or get hot with no load.
Decide: keep chargers whole and plug them into 12V sockets (easiest, swappable), or open them and wire the boards directly (compact). Note which wire is + on each.
Mount the sockets or boards on the board with gaps between them for air. They get warm at full load.
Run a positive and a negative bus wire past every socket. On 12V sockets the centre contact is positive and the outer shell is negative.
steps.warn: Reversed polarity kills most chargers instantly. Check with the multimeter before plugging anything in.

steps.text: Fit the fuse holder within 30 cm of battery positive. Size: number of ports × 1–1.5A at 12V, e.g. 4 ports → 7.5A fuse. Leave the fuse out while wiring.
steps.warn: An unfused wire from a battery can melt and start a fire if it shorts.

steps.text: Add the switch and voltmeter on the positive line after the fuse.

For bare buck boards: power them up with nothing plugged in and turn the trim screw until the output reads 5.1V. Then short the two middle USB pins (D+ and D−) together at each socket so most phones will accept full current.
Insert the fuse, plug in phones one at a time, and check each charges. After 30 minutes at full load, feel each charger and the wiring: warm is fine, too hot to hold is not.
Label the station with the fuse size and keep it out of rain. Switch it off when not charging; idle chargers still draw a little.

notes:
## Power maths
- A USB port at full load: 5V × 2.1A ≈ 10.5W. At about 85% efficiency that draws roughly 1A from a 12V battery.
- A phone charge is about 10–20Wh. A 12V 7Ah battery (about 40Wh usable) charges 2–4 phones. A 100Ah battery (about 600Wh usable) charges 30–60.
- Fuse: total 12V current × 1.25, rounded up to a standard size. Wire: 16 AWG for up to about 8A over 2 m, 14 AWG for more.

## Why car chargers
Phones only draw full current when the charger tells them they may, through the data pins. Car chargers do this already. Bare buck boards don't; shorting D+ to D− works for most Android phones (about 1.5A). Some phones still charge slowly from bare boards.

## Bare buck boards
- LM2596-type boards: 4.5–40V in, up to about 2A continuous without extra cooling.
- Always set the output voltage before connecting a phone. A new board's trim pot may be set anywhere.
- A board fed from 24V runs hotter than from 12V.

## Protecting the battery
Lead-acid: stop at about 12.0V (under light load) to avoid damage. A voltmeter is the simplest guard. A low-voltage cut-off board or a solar controller's load output does it for you.

## Variations
- Feed it straight from a solar panel? Only through a battery or a solar controller's load output. A bare panel's voltage sags and swings, and phones stop and start charging.
- From 24V systems, car chargers rated 12–24V work; check the label.

## If you lack a part
- No 12V sockets: open the car chargers and solder wires to their tip (+) and side spring (−).
- No fuse holder: an inline blade fuse from a car's wiring loom works; or a short length of thin wire as a fusible link, as a last resort.
